title: No work, no food
hookLine: the Chan master Baizhang: a day without work is a day without food (Chan tradition)
last: HARM INTO THE HANDS OF SOMEONE ELSE.

cards: The tools are gone. The hoe, the rake, whatever he used in the fields, hidden by his own students. They meant well.
Their teacher was old, the Chan tradition says, and still went out every day to work the land beside the monks, and they wanted him to rest. He didn't argue. He didn't search.
He just didn't eat that day. When they asked why, his answer has been passed down in Chan and Zen communities: a day without work is a day without food. The teacher was Baizhang.
Today's word is the first half of his saying.

teach.h: A CHAN MASTER IN THE FIELDS.
teach.b: First, who Baizhang is in the story. Chan is the Chinese school of Buddhism known in Japan as Zen.
Tradition remembers Baizhang as a Chan master who shaped how a monastery ran day to day: when to sit, when to eat, when to work. In this telling, the monks didn't only meditate.
They farmed, cooked, swept and hauled, and the teacher worked with them. Second, what the saying is not. No work, no food can sound like a threat a boss might shout.

teach.h: A RULE HE KEPT FOR HIMSELF.
teach.b: But in the story, Baizhang says it of himself. Nobody punishes him; he simply keeps his own rule. The sharpness is aimed inward.
Third, a difference worth saying plainly.

teach.h: ALMS, OR THE HOE: BOTH FEED.
teach.b: In other Buddhist communities, monks live on alms, food given by lay people, and that giving is itself a practice for the givers.
The Chan way of working the land grew up alongside that, as a different arrangement, not a correction of it. Both keep a community fed and a mind awake. Fourth, what it might mean at a kitchen table.
In a monastery, work is shared, and nobody's job is beneath anyone. Somebody washes the pots, and the teacher might be the one with his sleeves rolled up.
At home, the same question waits by the sink.
Baizhang's saying doesn't ask you to earn your dinner in money. It asks whether you've done your share of what keeps the place running.

how: In Chan and Zen monasteries, monks and teachers share manual work such as cooking, cleaning and gardening as part of daily practice, and Baizhang's saying is often quoted about it.

o: half of a rule a Chan teacher kept for himself
a monastery punishment for monks who skipped chores
a Chinese proverb about saving grain for winter

games.q: the story of Baizhang — tap the pairs.
p: a day without work, a day without food
the Chinese school later called Zen

s: in the story, Baizhang uses the saying to punish lazy monks
he says it of himself, after his own tools were hidden.
in the telling, the teacher worked in the fields with the monks
the monastery's work was shared, and the teacher took part.
the saying is about earning money for dinner
the lesson read it as doing your share of the shared work.

games.q: you're Baizhang. you're old, and your students have hidden your tools so you'll rest. what do you do?
o: thank them and take the day off.
search the monastery until you find them.
games.why: the tradition says he simply didn't eat, and explained: a day without work is a day without food. a rule kept for himself, not for them.

practice: Think of one thing you wish others at home would do, rinse the cup, put the shoes away, and notice the small heat of that wish without scolding it.
Then turn it around, the way Baizhang did: make it a quiet rule for you alone, just for today, told to nobody, and hold it while the breath comes and goes.
If you pray, you can bring your household into it in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: No work. The first half of Baizhang's saying, a day without work is a day without food: a rule he kept for himself. Today's word.
